summary: A report from a joint W3C and IETF planning group that clarifies how URIs, URLs and URNs relate to one another and how URI schemes and URN namespaces get registered. It also lists open issues and makes recommendations. It is informational, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: People argued over whether web addresses and permanent names were different things. This report explains how the words fit together, like clarifying that every street address is a kind of location.

questions: what is the difference between url and urn
what is a urn namespace id
subtitle: A planning group's attempt to untangle what URI, URL and URN mean and how schemes and namespaces get registered.

tldr.problem: Documents about web identifiers used URI, URL and URN in ways that seemed interchangeable or contradictory, and the registries for schemes and namespaces were incomplete.
tldr.mechanism: The report contrasts a classical view (a URI is either a URL or a URN) with a contemporary view (URI schemes, with URL as an informal idea), surveys registration, and lists recommendations.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational report with recommendations, not a specification, and it asks the W3C and IETF to adopt the contemporary model.

today: RFC 3305 is Informational and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the state of URI, URL and URN registration as of August 2002 and the group's recommendations.

sections.title: The W3C URI Interest Group
sections.content: In October 2000 the W3C formed a planning group to evaluate opportunities for W3C work on Uniform Resource Identifiers and to propose continued work. The group had W3C members and invited experts from the IETF. This report is its set of recommendations to both organisations.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of experts from two organisations met to sort out a naming mess and wrote down their advice.

sections.title: Classical and Contemporary Views
sections.content:
In the early to mid 1990s, people assumed an identifier fell into a class. It either gave the location of a resource (a URL) or its name, independent of location (a URN). A third class, URC for citations or metadata, was proposed but never got buy-in. So http: was a URL scheme and isbn: would someday be a URN scheme.

The contemporary view drops that partition. http: is a URI scheme, and so is urn:, which defines subspaces called namespaces. In urn:isbn:n-nn-nnnnnn-n, isbn is a namespace identifier, not a scheme. A URL is now an informal concept: a URI that identifies a resource through its primary access mechanism, such as its network location. An http URI is a URL.

The body of RFCs spans both periods. One speaks of URI schemes (RFC 2396), another of URL schemes (RFC 2717), another of URN schemes (RFC 2276). Experts use the terms interchangeably, but the wider community is not convinced they mean the same thing, and RFC 2396 section 1.2 did not clear it up.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago people sorted identifiers into two boxes, addresses and names. Now they say there is one big box of identifiers, and an address is just a kind that says where something is.

sections.title: Registering URI Schemes
sections.content:
The official register of scheme names is kept by IANA. At publication it listed 34 schemes, plus a few reserved names that were dropped. A separate list of known public schemes, registered or not, held 85, and about 50 of those were unregistered. Some are obsolete: phone was superseded by tel. Private schemes are probably impossible to count, though 1997 IETF minutes mention possibly 20 to 40 at Microsoft and 24 at WebTV.

RFC 2717 sets the registration procedure and RFC 2718 gives guidelines, although both say URL where they mean URI. The IETF tree is for schemes of general interest and needs the syntax and semantics published in an RFC. Alternative trees would have a . in the scheme name, but none was registered at that time and a vendor tree (vnd) was pending.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of allowed address types, but many are in use that never got on the list.

sections.title: Registering URN Namespaces
sections.content:
A URN namespace is identified by a Namespace ID (NID) registered with IANA. Informal NIDs have the form urn-<number>, and four existed: urn-1 to urn-4. Ten formal NIDs were listed: ietf, pin, issn, oid, newsml, oasis, xmlorg, publicid, isbn and nbn. The report notes there is no reliable way to find pending requests or their status. It also notes that hdl is used without being registered, perhaps because the owners were unsure whether to register it as a URI scheme or a URN namespace.

RFC 2611 describes how to get an NID. A request should cover identifier structure, character encoding rules, uniqueness, delegation of assignment, persistence, quality of service, resolution, lexical equivalence, URN syntax conformance, validation and scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming clubs for permanent names also have a sign-up list, but the waiting list is hard to see and some clubs never signed up.

sections.title: Open Issues and Recommendations
sections.content:
Two unresolved issues are flagged: URIs that identify things which are not network resources, such as an abstract object, a book or a person, and IRIs, an extension of URI syntax to non-ASCII.

The recommendations are:

  • The W3C and IETF jointly develop a model consistent with the contemporary view.
  • Generalise RFC 2717 and RFC 2718 to say URI schemes and move them forward as Best Current Practices.
  • Clarify registration for alternative trees in RFC 2717.
  • Register public schemes where possible, and purge or mark obsolete ones.
  • Update IANA: add urn to the URI schemes with a pointer to the namespace registry, track pending registrations, and label the page as the official registry.

The report says it raises no known security threats.
sections.plainLanguage: The group asks for one clear set of words, tidy lists, and a way to see what is waiting to be added.
